Pros:
1. Engaging Strategy: For The King offers a captivating blend of turn-based strategy and roguelike elements. The need for thoughtful planning and decision-making keeps players engrossed.
2. Co-op Gameplay: The multiplayer mode allows for seamless cooperation with friends, adding a layer of depth and camaraderie to the experience.
3. Unique Art Style: The game's visually appealing low-poly art style creates a charming and distinctive atmosphere that complements the fantasy setting.
4. Dynamic World: The procedurally generated maps and quests ensure that no two playthroughs are the same, providing a high level of replayability.
5. Deep Progression System: The leveling, equipment, and skill progression offer a satisfying sense of growth and customization for characters.

Cons:
1. Steep Learning Curve: New players might find the initial learning curve to be a bit steep, as understanding the various mechanics and strategies can take some time.
2. Randomness Factor: The procedural generation, while adding replayability, can occasionally lead to unbalanced encounters or quests.

Overview:
For The King is a delightful blend of strategy and roguelike elements that offers a fresh take on cooperative gameplay. Its engaging mechanics and charming art style create an immersive fantasy world that is as challenging as it is rewarding.

Gameplay:
The core gameplay of For The King revolves around turn-based combat and strategic decision-making. Players must navigate a procedurally generated world, complete quests, and battle a variety of foes. The inclusion of hex-based movement and positional tactics adds an extra layer of depth, requiring players to carefully plan their actions.

One standout feature is the seamless integration of both single-player and multiplayer modes. The cooperative experience shines, as players work together to overcome challenges and leverage each character's unique abilities. The game encourages communication and teamwork, making it a highly engaging experience for groups of friends.

Graphics and Sound:
For The King boasts a visually appealing low-poly art style that lends a distinctive charm to the game world. The environments are beautifully designed, and the character models are expressive, despite their simple geometry. The use of vibrant colors and dynamic lighting adds depth to the world, making exploration a visual treat.

The sound design complements the visuals perfectly. From the whimsical tunes in towns to the tense battle music, the soundtrack sets the tone for each situation. Sound effects, like the clashing of swords or the creaking of a ship, further immerse players in the world.

Story and Narrative:
While For The King doesn't prioritize an intricate narrative, it provides enough context to keep players invested in their journey. The overarching goal of vanquishing the chaos threatening the kingdom serves as a solid backdrop for the gameplay. Memorable moments arise from the unexpected twists and challenges encountered along the way.

Character development, though somewhat limited in terms of individual narratives, is driven by player choices and the progression system. As characters level up and acquire new equipment, they become more versatile, allowing for diverse strategies.

Performance and Technical Issues:
For The King runs smoothly overall, with short loading times and stable performance during gameplay. However, there were occasional instances of minor graphical glitches, such as objects clipping through terrain. These were infrequent and didn't significantly impact the experience.

Multiplayer and Community:
The multiplayer aspect of For The King shines, allowing for seamless online co-op. The game provides various options for connecting with friends, whether through Steam integration or by sharing a lobby code. The community surrounding the game is active and supportive, with forums and discussions readily available for those seeking advice or looking for others to play with.

Final Thoughts:
For The King is a standout title in the strategy and roguelike genres, offering an engaging cooperative experience with deep gameplay mechanics. While it may pose a slight learning curve for newcomers, the rewarding progression and dynamic world make it well worth the investment. With its charming art style and robust multiplayer features, For The King is a must-play for fans of tactical RPGs.

Pick up deluxe edition for the extra couple bucks as well as the items, two classes, and new campaign are worth the very tiny amount of extra money, about $1.50 on sale.

You have a wide range of classes to choose from which you can unlock as you play the game, although most of the classes don't seem particularly well balanced. Basically you're almost always going to be playing characters who have a high speed stat as they go first in combat, while those with lower speed only end up hindering you. Your damage isn't based on your class either, it's based on the weapon you're using. Only your stats which can help with accuracy and with getting better luck in the various random events, starting items, and passive skills are affected by your class, but ultimately speed reigns supreme which is a bit unfortunate. Plus nearly all of the classes play the game. There's no real difference between a strength-based character and an intellect-based character since all skills your characters have are based off the weapon you're using. A strength character could use an intellect weapon if they wanted to although they'd have very low accuracy with it. It would be nice if each class had some innate skills they could use regardless of their weapon (some like herbalist which has party heal do but its one of very few) rather than random passives that don't really mean too much. For example: The Blacksmith class being able to use a stun against an enemy no matter what weapon he's using as long as it's strength-based rather than it being complete rng what skills he'll get. I also wish that when you leveled up you could maybe get skill points to spend into extra health or damage or something instead of it just being a flat boost for all of your stats. That being said, I still do like skills being based off of weapons as it keeps things fresh as you play the game and replace your gear, I just wish it was a bit more complex.

The enemies and dungeons are well varied, and while the combat is very simply designed it's still quite fun and easily accessible for anyone unlike some other RPGs such as Divinity Original Sin (which is also a great turn-based RPG). It's rather neat that many enemies have special abilities like being able to destroy your items, steal money, or cause your character to flee combat. This however, sometimes can cause fights that are more difficult than they should be when you get an enemy that can destroy your gear, another that will steal your gold and flee with it, AND one that will do massive damage to your party, possibly killing someone all in the same fight.

The campaigns are all fairly enjoyable. The story is generic, but that's fine for a game like this. Each campaign has its own unique theme and mechanics, and combined with the random generation allows you to play multiple runs of the same maps and still experience something new, or at least, different. On top of being able to purchase new encounters on the map as you play, there's enough here to keep you entertained for a while. There's even an endless mode that's nothing but combat if that suits your fancy.

The balancing is a little off sometimes. I've mentioned classes already, but the rng in your campaigns can really screw you over as well. Entire runs can end because you didn't get a good enough gear drop and now you have outdated weapons and are unable to obtain new ones since you've cleared what dungeons you could and towns don't stock anything useful to you. Some status effects can completely cripple your run as well by nuking your stats or destroying good equipment you have. For the most part this hasn't been a problem for me, but it does happen on occasion, so make sure you keep backup gear with you instead of immediately selling it.

Overall, while not my favorite turn-based game it comes in a close second. It's a lot more fun to play with friends but still an enjoyable solo experience. I rate it an 85/100 due to it's cheap price tag and simple but enjoyable fun that provides a good challenge that isn't too bs... a fair amount of the time anyways. Points are deducted for your runs being heavily dictated by good rng and the necessity to grind at times in order to prepare for later parts of a campaign, and while for me this was only a problem some of the time I can very well see it being a lot more problematic for others depending on your luck. They are making a second For The King game, so it'll be exciting to see what they do with that when it comes out.

For the King is a great tabletop rogue-like adventure game. It supports up to 3 players but you can also play solo and control 3 characters. The game a has a lot of replayability with there because different campaigns you can run and different team comps you can build. 

Story-wise there isn't much. Like it introduces one and it's there, but it's there's not much to it and it's uninteresting. At least I felt that way. I honestly can't even remember what the main campaign was about. 

This game is entirely based on RNG and that's a huge turn off for some people. Most of the negative reviews are because this is the way the game is structured. If you like trying to maximize your RNG chances or succeeding a 20% chance roll then I highly recommend this game. If you don't like the concept of RNG controlling everything then maybe stay away. Even if you aren't too good at the game there's a lot of game rule modifiers that make the game a lot easier. 

I have yet to encounter any bugs in this game except the ones that attack you. 

I think my main complaint for this game would be that, generally, you need to follow a balanced team comp of: healer, damage, and tank, to actually win. There's different comps you can try and still beat the game with but on the harder difficulties something like a full damage team won't work.
Think of it as a board game, but in the best possible way. Amazing re-playability, fun solo, fun multi, just fun.

For the first 6 hours my friends and I had a great time, the game was a challenge but it was enjoyable and fair. But at some point in the game, the enemies just become super overwhelming. It feels like they are playing a different game then we are playing. 

Our "heroes" just feel like regular townsfolk who wondered too far out of the village while every enemy has 40 dmg AOE abilities that add a burn and take away your focus. Don't worry you can use your very limited God's beards that end up costing 200-300 gold at level 10 to heal every turn so you don't die. Every enemy is immune to 8 things, has physical and magical shields, and hardly ever miss their rolls. 

In my opinion, this game doesn't need to be a rouge-like. The game feels very long and tedious which is fine in a classic RPG adventure, but not in a game you have to restart when you die. Our 9 hour first run has exhausted me and my buddies. We don't feel satisfied about the 9 hours, in fact we feel like they were wasted, which makes us not want to start another run at all. I think this game is awesome, i really like turn based games and one i can play with friends is just icing on the cake. But with how much dice rolling and time each run takes, its just much too exhausting to put the hours in to get a lucky run to make it all the way. Give us a way to turn off the rogue elements and i would have a much better time spending hours and hours developing my character.

I have been a "hardcore mode" and rougelike fanatic for over a decade, and have thousands of hours logged across dozens of titles. I've lost many, MANY runs and had characters die on which I had spent weeks of my life. I say all this to give you some perspective, so you don't think I'm just "mad because I'm bad".
This title has so much potential, but as it is now the game has several mechanics which are frustrating, un-fun and in my opinion, inherently incompatible with each other and the genre as a whole. 

Point #1: A single run in this game is Loooooong. Of my 18hrs. of playtime, more than 14 was spent on a single campaign from beginning to final boss. Not only that, but much of your time is spent clicking around the overworld trying to scrape together enough gold to buy gear and supplies for the next boss dungeon. (Grinding)

Point #2: The turn based combat has very little depth or strategy. There are two types of damage in the game, Physical and Magic. Some enemies are resistant to physical, some magical. 90% of your turns are going to be doing the same middling attack with the highest accuracy rating against the weakest enemy. "But wait!" you might exclaim,"What about the 50 status ailments, buffs and debuffs in the game? Surely they provide some spice and variety? Surely you would want to cast other spells and use other abilities?"
To which I would reply, "Nope." and in Point #3 I will tell you why.

Point #3: Risk aversion & Action economy are the two biggest forces that will drive your decisions in game, and you will constantly be forced to skip events or play it safe in combat because [i]the penalty for whiffing a roll is way too high[/i]. I learned this lesson the hard way a few hours into my very first run. I saved up enough gold to buy a nice boat, set sail and happened upon a "Nice fishing spot". I made the mistake of accepting a random roll with unknown outcomes and next thing I know, the Kraken had destroyed my boat and shipwrecked my entire party. I ended up out 200 gold, wasting 5 turns, and a permanent -1 to all stats for each hero. I don't know what the positive outcomes were, but if it was in line with other events I probably would have found a free item of medium-low value. Many other events are similarly not worth the risk.
Likewise in combat, as I mentioned earlier, every single special effect, debuff or buff [i]without exception[/i] requires a perfect roll to take effect. It has proven to never be worth attempting these abilities, because when you fail, your entire turn is wasted. It is also usually never worth it to switch weapons because that eats an entire turn as well. Staying in combat for as few rounds as possible and minimizing damage is key to survival as the devs did not see fit to include combat healing magic. Every point of HP you need to heal will cost you consumables or gold.

What it feels like: Picture this scenario - You're 8 hours into the run, just sailed across the ocean in high spirits after beating the area's boss. You pick up a bounty from the next capital city and head off into the wilds to fight some monsters. You spend a couple of hours slaying overworld mobs and mini-dungeons until you can finally afford that upgraded wand and boots in town. Now that you are ready you head down to the next boss dungeon. On floor three you get crit twice, everyone is on fire and one person is petrified. One failed armor buff roll and a failed taunt roll later, everyone goes down, run over. Guess you should have spent another hour grinding to buy some more consumables.

Final thoughts: No one wants to devote this much time to a roguelike run. No one wants to lose a run to events they felt were beyond their control. I personally don't want to play a game where you never get to make real and impactful decisions, you just roll the dice and hope for the best. With a little reworking this game could be great, but as it stands now it is not worth buying.

This game.  Where to start?

Pros:

* highly addictive gameplay with outstanding rpg mechanics.

* good loot system with paper doll equipped items and well designed item attributes.

* cool-looking procedurally generated hex grid map.

* the few wins you achieve will be extremely satisfying!

Cons:

* You are VERY unlikely to beat this game (even on easiest difficulty) without a good number of unlocks.  Be prepared to grind a few losses to build up your lore (currency for unlocking characters, items, and events).

* I'm 100 hours in and have yet to beat the game on Journeyman difficulty which is one step up from easiest difficulty.  The game is designed to beat you, troll you, and enrage you (HULK SMASH !!!).

* combat UI is a bit wonky, but is servicable once you get used to it.


More gory details:

Saw this streamed on Twitch and decided it was worth (part of Steam Holiday sale).  After first few playthroughs on easiest difficutly I was questioning my purchase.  I pride myself a gamer... why am I getting my bootie handed to me so hard?  Is the game rigged?  What's up with my Hunter only proc'ing his passive (automatic crit) when the enemy has 1 hp?  Cool - the game has gelatinous cubes !  wait... did it just dissolve my armor ???!!!  Why are my weapons so sucky?  Why is everything so expensive at the markets and vendors?

I had many questions, and few solutions.  But, after a few more games and my first victory, I was hooked for good.  Presently, after calming myself from my latest rage quit, I grind away at Journeyman difficulty trying different party compositions and laughing/crying/raging when the game trolls me.


If you enjoy rogue-like games, rpgs, challenging strategy scenarios, and can sometimes appreciate it when you are being trolled by the developers then do NOT hesitate - buy this game immediately.
